extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, scholars, policymakers, and Federal Circuit Bar Journal readers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains statutory definitions, standards, and procedural rules from the legislative history of the America Invents Act (AIA) as they affect patentability, post-grant review, stays, funding, deceptive-intent rules, and patent-term adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business method patent' — financial products/services
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18's covered business method patent definition encompasses patents that claim a 'financial product or service' and is intended to be broader than just traditional banking operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative statements clarify that 'financial product or service' is not limited to banks but includes insurance, brokerages, mutual funds, annuities, and an array of financial companies outside traditional banking. Senators noted the provision targets patents describing steps used in everyday business applications in financial products and retail services. (Sen. Leahy, Sen. Schumer, Sen. Cantwell statements cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business method patent' — 'data processing or other operations'
rubrics_metrics.description: The House amendment broadened earlier Senate language limited to 'data processing operations' to 'data processing or other operations,' thereby expanding the scope beyond Class 705.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate language originally tracked Class 705; insertion of the word 'other' was intended to ensure section 18 reaches business-method patents issued in other classifications. The legislative history emphasizes that the change broadens the definition beyond mere class 705 patents. (Statements of Sen. Cantwell and Sen. Schumer.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Method or corresponding apparatus' covers many claim types
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18's phrase 'a method or corresponding apparatus' is meant to encompass any type of claim in a patent regardless of claim structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sen. Schumer explained this phrase was intended to include method claims, system claims, apparatus claims, graphical user interface claims, data structure (Lowry) claims, and storage-media (Beauregard) claims. The point: clever drafting should not avoid PTO review—substance over form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18 post-grant review institution threshold ('more likely than not')
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 incorporates the post-grant review threshold: the petitioner must present information which, if not rebutted, would demonstrate that it is more likely than not that a claim is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high evidentiary threshold (strong showing) used for post-grant review; it does not require raising a 'substantial new question of patentability' as in pre-AIA inter partes reexamination. The Director may institute review on issues previously considered by an examiner if persuaded the examiner erred. Also allows institution on a showing that 'the petition raises a novel or unsettled legal question that is important to other patents or patent applications.' (AIA sec. 6(d)/§324(a)–(b) and related legislative discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No statutory requirement for PTO deference to district court decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal requirement that the USPTO give deference or weight to a district court's decision regarding a patent's validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and Federal Circuit precedent (In re Swanson) indicate a prior district court judgment upholding validity does not prevent the PTO from finding claims unpatentable. PTO and courts use different standards, purposes, parties, and outcomes; thus a court decision is not binding on PTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards of proof and claim construction in PTO proceedings vs district courts
rubrics_metrics.description: PTO proceedings apply a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard and give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification, whereas district courts apply clear-and-convincing evidence and different claim-construction approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the standard of proof is lower in PTO review, and because claim construction and issues considered differ between forums, the same evidence may lead to different outcomes in PTO proceedings versus district court litigation. This explains why previous court findings are not determinative for PTO review. (In re Swanson discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stays of litigation under AIA §18(b) — Broadcast Innovation four-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA §18(b)(1) codifies a four-factor test (the Broadcast Innovation test) federal courts must use when considering a stay of infringement litigation because a §18 proceeding was instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history emphasizes the fourth Broadcast Innovation factor—whether a stay will reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and the court—and states the codified test precludes additional, non-codified factors (e.g., forgoing certain invalidity arguments). Senators characterized the provision as strongly favoring stays; absent exceptional circumstances, institution of a business-method proceeding should substitute for litigation and lead to a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeals and appellate standard for stays (Federal Circuit review)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA §18(b)(2) authorizes immediate interlocutory appeal from a district court's decision on a stay, directing the Federal Circuit to review to ensure consistent application of established precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history states the Federal Circuit should review such stay decisions de novo (unless unique circumstances recommend otherwise) to ensure uniform application and to avoid forum-shopping. 'Established precedent' is intended to limit referenced caselaw to that applying the Broadcast Innovation four factors in combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of deceptive-intent restrictions (AIA §20)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA §20 repealed provisions in title 35 that barred a patent owner from using certain authorities or defenses if prior applicant actions were deemed tainted by 'deceptive intent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sen. Kyl and legislative history state the repeal moves the patent system away from subjective-intent focus toward an objective, evidence-based system, reducing litigation cost and administrative burden. Repeals affect corrections to inventorship, retroactive foreign filing licenses, section 251 reissue, and enforcement of remaining claims when one claim is invalidated due to deceptive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on §288 and inequitable-conduct doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to §288 (via AIA §20) provide that whenever a claim of a patent is invalid, an action may be maintained for infringement of a claim of the patent which may be valid—i.e., repeal of deceptive-intent bars should limit infectious invalidity caused by inequitable conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history notes ambiguity because §288 speaks of a claim that is 'invalid', while inequitable conduct traditionally leads to 'unenforceability.' Historically, courts construed §288's 'without deceptive intention' requirement to bar enforcement if any claim was invalid by reason of fraud (Kearney & Trecker; Chromalloy). The repeal aims to protect otherwise untainted valid claims, but its precise scope and interaction with modern inequitable-conduct doctrine may be uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO funding and revolving fund (AIA §22) — procedural/administrative treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA §22 restates pre-AIA law about depositing USPTO user fees in the Treasury and reflects compromise over creating a USPTO revolving fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final bill removed the revolving fund that would have given direct USPTO access to fees. As a compromise, appropriators pledged to give the USPTO full access to its user fees via appropriations language, including making excess collections 'available until expended.' Legislative history recounts the political fight over fee diversion and the practical impacts on USPTO planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default effective date for AIA provisions (AIA §35)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA §35 establishes a default effective date: provisions without their own effective-date provision take effect one year after enactment and apply to any patent issued on or after that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some rules (e.g., the new advice-of-counsel rule) lacked explicit effective dates, they fall under this default. The provision clarifies the timing for application of AIA changes to patents issued after the effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation and timeliness rules for patent-term-extension (PTE) deadlines (AIA §37)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA §37 amends the calculation of the PTE filing deadline under 35 U.S.C. §156(d)(1): the patentee must seek extension within the 60-day period beginning on the date the product received permission for commercial marketing or use; PTE filings received on weekends, holidays, or after 4:30 P.M. ET are deemed received on the next business day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision applies retroactively to any PTE application pending or subject to judicial review at the AIA's enactment (e.g., the Angiomax PTE). The practical effect is to prevent inadvertent forfeiture where approval occurs late in the day or on a non-business day; the legislative and floor debate reveal political controversy over perceived special-interest 'fixes.'
